Entertainment.title: Woman says she was left 'bewildered and confused' by alleged Russell Brand assault
Entertainment.text:
Warning - this report contains graphic content

A woman who alleges she was indecently assaulted by Russell Brand has told his trial she was left feeling "bewildered and confused".

The woman, who worked at MTV at the time, said the entertainer went from "jovial" to a "wild-eyed maniac" as he attempted, she alleged, to pull her into a toilet.

Brand, 51, faces seven charges in the trial - three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault.

The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges.

The woman gave evidence on Friday from behind a screen at Southwark Crown Court in London, on the third day of Brand's trial.

She told the jury the alleged incident at MTV lasted for about 20 seconds, adding: "It was a very short exchange."

Asked how she felt after the alleged attack by Brand, the woman said: "Bewildered, confused, 'what the hell happened there?'"

She said Brand went from someone who was "affable" to a "wild-eyed maniac trying to pull me into the toilet".

"I was confused that that actually just happened - anyone would be," she said.

The complainant told jurors on Friday she met Brand in 2001 when she worked at MTV.

She said she recognised him straight away and said there was "banter" between them initially.

After noticing his "distinctive T-shirt" with the words "I am Spartacus", she told Brand she "loved it" and wanted it.

"He said, 'you can have it'", the woman told the jury, to which she said she replied: "Make sure it gets a good wash first."

Brand then asked her for directions to the bathroom.

The woman, who was in her thirties at the time, said she offered to show him the way because she was going in the same direction.

Prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC asked her what happened next.

She said his "demeanour changed" when they got to the bathroom door.

"He grabbed my forearm, he was leaning into the door and he was quite forceful," she said, adding that it took her "unaware".

Asked by the prosecutor what she meant by his demeanour changing, the witness said: "He grabbed me by the arm, started to pull me in."

She said Brand then said to her "come on" while still holding her forearm.

The woman said while Brand was trying to pull her into the bathroom, she was trying to pull herself away.

"I said to him, 'What are you doing, are you mad, let me go'... and then he started to... plead almost," she said.

The woman told the court she managed to "wrench" herself from Brand's grip because of her own strength.

She told jurors Brand went from "jovial, affable, friendly to suddenly turning into this wild-eyed manic so I was quite confused this was happening, as anyone would be".

Asked by the prosecutor why she did not report what had happened to her employer, she said: "I was scared... I thought it would be my word against his."

But she did tell two of her colleagues, she said.

Jurors heard that she reported the allegation to the police in 2023 after watching a Channel 4 documentary about Brand.

"I thought it was the right thing to do to come forward," she told the court.

Brand's barrister challenged the complainant on the fact that she did not report Brand for what he had allegedly done until after watching the documentary.

"You didn't think there was any need to report him," Ian Winter KC said.

"It would have been my word against his," she replied. "He didn't manage to rape me. I managed to get out of the situation."

The defence barrister said: "It was only after you saw the television programme that you think he was trying to rape you in the toilet."

The woman responded: "Why else would you drag someone into the toilet if you weren't going to assault them."

Winter KC continued: "Twenty-two years before that, you hadn't thought he was trying to get you in there to rape you..."

The woman denied that, adding: "You don't grab someone by the arm. You don't grip someone and try to drag them in, that's not consensual."

The woman was speaking after a former flatmate of Brand's, Andrew Dobson, earlier told the jury that "sex was a huge preoccupation" for the entertainer.

Dobson gave evidence after another woman told the court on Thursday that Russell Brand raped her in a hotel room in Bournemouth in 1999.

She said she had met Brand, before he was famous, while she was attending the Labour Party conference.

Dobson told the court on Friday he attended the Bournemouth conference and had written music for a fringe event that Brand was part of.

Karmy-Jones asked Dobson how he would describe Brand's character as he got to know him before he was famous.

Dobson told the court Brand was a "very vibrant character, very egotistical".

"I would say lively," he continued. "Sort of quite demanding and persuasive. I think erratic would be maybe a slightly better term."

Dobson also told the court that "sex was a huge preoccupation for him", referring to Brand.

He said he recalled a couple of nights when "clearly the pursuit of getting somebody in bed would be a preoccupation" for Brand.

The jury heard that Dobson was staying in the same guesthouse with Brand and other cast members.

The morning after Brand is alleged to have raped a woman, he returned to the place where some of the cast had been staying, the jury heard.

Asked by the prosecutor to describe the "circumstances of how he came home", Dobson replied: "My primary recollection is very hurried and rushed... I recall Russell coming in and suddenly an urgency we had to leave, things being really hurried".

The prosecutor asked the witness: "Where did urgency come from?"

Dobson replied: "I can't recall anything specific that was said. I only remember the atmosphere and panicked, urgent. Feeling tense and confusing."

He went on to tell the jury there had been an "abrupt change of atmosphere" from what had been a "fun week" to an "abrupt change of tone".

Under cross-examination by Brand's barrister, it was put to Dobson that in his witness statement he said that Brand was one of few men he knew that women would swoon over.

Dobson replied: "He was certainly charismatic".

Brand denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty.

He has said that any sexual contact if it happened, would have been consensual.

The trial continues.

Entertainment.title: Judge tosses child sex abuse charges against actor Timothy Busfield
Entertainment.text:
A judge in the US state of New Mexico has thrown out charges against Emmy-winning actor Timothy Busfield on Friday, saying there were issues with how prosecutors presented the case.

The West Wing and Field of Dreams actor was indicted in February on four counts of criminal sexual contact of a child. Busfield has denied all allegations.

The charges stemmed from accusations brought by child actors he worked with on the Fox series The Cleaning Lady, which he directed and produced.

The judge said on Friday that the prosecutor "failed to act in a fair and impartial manner". The district attorney's office said it is evaluating options on how to move forward.

State District Judge Joseph Montano granted the defence's motion to dismiss the indictment on Friday, citing mistakes that undermined the grand jury process.

"Our office has received the order and is evaluating our options to determine how we will proceed," a spokesperson for the Office of the Second Judicial District Attorney in Bernalillo County told the BBC on Friday.

The BBC has contacted a legal representative for Busfield.

The actor surrendered to state authorities in January when a warrant was issued for his arrest. A judge later ordered his release pending trial.

Busfield had originally been taken into custody in Albuquerque on two counts of criminal sexual contact with a minor and one count of child abuse.

The indictment against him, reviewed by the BBC, said that on or between 19 October 2022 and 10 September 2023, Busfield "touched or applied force to the intimate parts" of one of the unnamed boys when he was under the age of 13.

The Thirtysomething actor's defence team submitted more than 70 letters from people vouching for his character and said that he underwent and passed a polygraph test pertaining to the allegations against him.

In a warrant for Busfield's arrest, prosecutors had said the parents of the boys alleged that he groomed and sexually abused the youngsters while working on The Cleaning Lady.

Authorities claimed the boys referred to Busfield as "Uncle Tim" and alleged that he "would tickle them on the stomach and legs". Both boys told authorities they were touched inappropriately for years, his arrest affidavit stated.

Busfield's lawyers had said the actor was being accused as an act of revenge after the children were fired from the series, which angered their mother.

The BBC's Nardine Saad contributed to this report.

Entertainment.title: Halloween costumes 2026: From Obsession to Odyssey, the top TV, film and pop culture party outfits
Entertainment.text:
If you're still on the hunt for the perfect Halloween costume, then you might want to look to gargoyles, Freaky Nikki and Dolly Parton for inspiration - they are all predicted to be popular outfit choices for 2026.

"People don't necessarily want to look frightening - they want to look extraordinary," says costume designer Tamar Zaig, who runs a fancy dress hire shop in London and says she's seeing a "real appetite for escapism, glamour and a bit of dark humour" right now.

And as usual, the year's major film and TV releases, as well as news and pop culture trends, are also driving outfit choices.

So, here are some spooky ideas to try.

The Traitors is a timely choice, with host Claudia Winkleman's look easy to pull together. Think fringe, tartan, chunky knitwear and some heavy eyeliner.

Winkleman is "a classic that we see every year", says the creator behind the popular Love of Huns Instagram account (who did not want to be named). But she "will definitely be making a return this Halloween off the back of all the Traitors love and the icon that she is".

Ice hockey romance series Off Campus also features in many of the outfit inspiration videos trending online.

The show's main characters, Dean and Allie attend a Halloween party in the series, with Allie dressed as J-Lo and Dean as Top Gun's Maverick, which could provide a rather meta costume opportunity for fans or couples.

Another of this year's most popular TV shows, Widow's Bay - which scooped up at this year's Emmy Awards - is also inspiring outfits.

Maria Nichol, 35, a horror aficionado from Ely in Cambridgeshire, plans to dress as Kate O'Flynn's character Patricia - and is trying to replicate her gothic headdress, which includes antlers and a taxidermy fox, by crafting her own from foam clay, foil and fur.

One of the most replicated outfits looks set to be Nikki from indie horror film phenomenon Obsession, say fancy dress shops, influencers and make-up artists.

The character's red and black zebra print top went viral earlier this year, selling out online and reportedly leading to a 27,000-person waitlist, external before returning to stores.

"We've had customers asking for Nikki," says Muhammad Rai from shop Fancy Dress Town in London, with people trying to recreate her with a red corset and wig, "although unfortunately, we currently have none in stock".

"I've had a few people ask me to do that make-up for them," adds special effects make-up artist and prosthetics designer Meg, from Liverpool.

"I'm seeing a lot of Gothic romance and historical influences not only in films such as Wuthering Heights, The Odyssey and The Bride!, but in fashion too, with corsets, lace, dramatic silhouettes appearing on the catwalks, particularly at London Fashion Week," says designer Zaig.

"Along with Peaky Blinders, I think these kind of productions have brought some great theatrical costume styles back into the spotlight, from elaborate period gowns and Greek mythology to 1930s glamour."

Classic horror franchises such as Scream and Scary Movie (Scream 7 and Scary Movie 6 were both released this year), should also not be overlooked, say fancy dress shops.

Ghost face masks from Scream have made up 30% of sales at Hollywood Fancy Dress in Bournemouth, says the shop's head manager Ben Cook.

Meanwhile, characters from hit series Wednesday and Bridgerton are likely to make a return. And outfits from KPop Demon Hunters – which won best animated film at this year's Oscars - are the current biggest seller for children, according to Cook.

It's not just fictional characters who might be joining your Halloween night out.

"I also expect to see plenty of instantly recognisable personalities, from the iconic Dolly Parton with her extravagant wigs and rhinestones to political figures such as Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin," says Zaig.

Rai from Fancy Dress Town also says blonde wigs, cowboy-style waistcoats and microphones are in high demand, following the death of Parton aged 80 in August.

The whimsical fashion trend, which has dominated social media feeds in 2026, is also predicted to be a big influence this Halloween for women. Think gargoyles, moths, mushrooms, woodland fairies and 17th Century Pierrot clowns.

In keeping with the theme, Lauren Sidebottom, a TikTok beauty and fashion creator from Leeds, is planning on dressing up as a weeping angel.

The 23-year-old, who studied theatrical makeup at college, says she'll be creating the look using body paint, grey tights, a cracking makeup effect on her skin, drawn-on tears, and a grey wig.

Women her age are, she says "wanting to look cool, different, not like every other girl," with their whimsical costumes.

Tiggy Bellinger, 21, from West Sussex, agrees DIY costumes can help avoid people wearing "the exact same thing".

She has also been sharing whimsical Halloween looks online, including a mime artist, the Very Hungry Caterpillar and a ladybird.

She uses clothes she already has or can borrow, and a bit of creative DIY, to create her looks, with the aim of encouraging others to do the same instead of buying ready-made outfits from fast fashion retailers.

"The fun thing about making costumes and Halloween is the creativity and finding bits and pieces that match and, you know, making things," she says.

This is also the case for Sophia, 25, who lives in Cambridge and is using a long blonde wig and pink dress she already owns to dress up as Hannah Montana, to chime with this year's anniversary special.

"Even if you just notice that you have one colour, like, 'Wow I have a lot of purple' or 'I have a lot of this sparkly material that I don't get to wear often', and thinking about what characters or what object even that that could remind you of, I think you could get something really creative that other people wouldn't have."

Entertainment.title: 'Well-known' man asks court to stop publication of sexual offence allegation
Entertainment.text:
An individual described as "well-known" has asked London's High Court to prevent two media organisations from publishing "serious allegations", including of a sexual nature, against him.

The court heard he had submitted medical evidence saying that if the allegations were made public this would "almost certainly" lead to him "attempting to take his own life", and that the prospect of publication had already led to two suicide attempts.

The court was told that Independent Television News and Guardian News & Media had carried out an investigation into the individual's "conduct over a period of years".

The individual, who has been granted anonymity in the court proceedings, denies the allegations.

The court was told that following an investigation that ITN, which produces news for ITV and Channel 4, and Guardian News & Media, which publishes the Guardian, sent two letters to the the well-known individual in the spring of 2026.

As well as denying the allegations, the individual responded with medical reports stating that there was a risk to his life if the information was published.

At an injunction hearing at London's High Court, lawyers representing ITN and Guardian News & Media said that "it would be wrong" for the court to "restrain publication" when the "law provides for a detailed and well-established scheme by which the interests of those at risk of suicide is specially protected by NHS mental health professionals".

The court has also granted anonymity to other individuals in the case.

Two individuals who have agreed to be identified in any ITN and Guardian News & Media report concerning the allegations were given anonymity in the current proceedings by High Court judge Mr Justice Nicklin. The nature of the allegations or how these two journalistic sources relate to them is not known.

A third journalistic source for the ITN and Guardian News & Media investigation has also been granted anonymity in the current proceedings. She has alleged that she was the victim of a sexual offence by the well-known individual.

The court will decide whether the ITN and Guardian News & Media will be permanently prevented from naming the well-known individual and publishing the allegations against him at a trial due to be held later this month.

Entertainment.title: Sean 'Diddy' Combs moves from New Jersey prison to facility in Pennsylvania
Entertainment.text:
Sean "Diddy" Combs has been transferred from a New Jersey correctional facility to a prison in Pennsylvania, the US Federal Bureau of Prisons says.

The rap mogul was moved to FCI Allenwood Low on Friday, a prison official said, but declined to discuss why he was moved, citing privacy, safety, and security reasons.

"His transfer from one low-security facility to another is an important distinction," Combs' spokesman told the BBC, adding that the move "is consistent with a decision made with safety and security in mind".

Combs, 56, who was sentenced to 50 months behind bars, has asked an appeals court to release him from prison and overturn his conviction on two prostitution-related crimes.

Combs' spokesman, Juda S Engelmayer, did not comment on an Associated Press report, external that Combs had been living a "luxury lifestyle" behind bars in New Jersey or on reports swirling about his health and treatment in lockup.

The move comes about two weeks after NBC News, external reported that the Bad Boy Records co-founder had access to mobile phones, liquor and other contraband at Fort Dix, as well as allegations that he had paid inmates to cook, clean and make his bed for him, and give him massages. He was also involved in two fights, according to NBC.

"It's because of the disruptive behaviour," Jose Rojas, union secretary for local federal prison employees, told NBC News of the move. "He's been causing too much trouble over there."

NBC reported Combs was stripped of 41 days for good conduct, pushing back his scheduled release date, which is now listed in the prison's online records as 2 March 2028. He was originally expected to be released in January 2028.

Engelmayer said he appreciates that the Federal Bureau of Prisons is "taking the safety and security of Sean and everyone involved seriously" and "we are grateful for the attention being given to his well-being and hope he can continue serving his time without unnecessary disruption".

The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on the reports.

"For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or disciplinary sanctions," spokesman Donald Murphy said.

FCI Allenwood Low is a low-security federal correctional institution for male offenders that is about 155 miles (250 km) west of New York City.

The facility houses about 1,044 inmates, according to its website, a significantly smaller population than the one at Combs' previous facility, Fort Dix, of more than 4,200 inmates across two campuses. Allenwood also has medium and maximum security facilities nearby.

Entertainment.title: Dame Judi Dench joins call to keep Archers in Birmingham
Entertainment.text:
More than 100 current and former cast and crew members of The Archers, including Dame Judi Dench, have called on the BBC to keep the programme in Birmingham.

The appeal follows a decision to shelve plans for a dedicated studio at the broadcaster's new Digbeth headquarters.

Supporters say recording the drama elsewhere could affect its quality and future.

The BBC says the move is part of wider cost-saving measures and alternative options are being explored.

In a letter to director general Matt Brittin, actors, writers, directors and sound engineers argued that moving recordings away from the Midlands would have a "tangible impact" on the programme.

The letter compares the prospect to "Coronation Street leaving the north-west, or EastEnders leaving the south-east", adding that it risks "ripping out the heart of Ambridge".

Signatories said Birmingham had been central to the show's identity since it began and warned that separating cast and production teams could affect the way the programme is made.

"A flagship show deserves flagship facilities, from which both the BBC and the city of Birmingham would benefit for decades," the letter said.

It was signed by more than 100 current and former cast and crew members, including Dench, Felicity Jones and Kellie Bright, as well as representatives from Equity and the Writers' Guild.

The Archers, set in the fictional West Midlands village of Ambridge, celebrated its 75th anniversary earlier this year and has always been recorded in Birmingham.

The intervention follows the BBC's announcement that plans for a bespoke studio at its new Tea Factory headquarters in Digbeth would not go ahead.

The Worcestershire village of Inkberrow is believed to have inspired the show's fictional village of Ambridge, while The Old Bull Inn is closely associated with the show's pub, The Bull.

Entertainment.title: London suburban housing project wins top UK architecture award
Entertainment.text:
A suburban housing development in south London has won the UK's most prestigious architecture award, with judges praising its sensitive design and integration into the surrounding landscape.

Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, comprising 157 homes across five distinctive 13-sided blocks, was named winner of the 2026 Stirling Prize by the Royal Institute of British Architects (Riba).

Designed by Mary Duggan Architects and built with RUFF Architects, it combines affordable and private housing for Croydon Council.

Replacing a former car park on a challenging, sloping site that varies in height by eight metres (26ft), Riba president Chris Williamson praised the design as a "new approach to higher density development" creating "a new connection between the bustling Lion Green Road and a distinctive area of green parkland beyond".

Williamson told the BBC that until he went to study architecture he lived in a council estate in the East Midlands, "and every time I go back there all the council houses have been sold off, they're in private hands.

"Which in a way can be a good thing - we're in a homeowning democracy - but the sad thing is they haven't been replaced.

"Every time I go back - without getting too emotional - I think 'where would we have lived?'

"So to me that's why this particular project was important. I think a lot of people from that sort of background live in terrible accommodation - temporary accommodation which isn't safe or secure.

"These houses are fantastic and they're part of a mixed scheme so it's got a fantastic feel to it.

"For me it was a very inspirational, emotional, part of the process."

Duggan, who was brought up in south-west London, said the scheme "challenged conventional suburban housing layouts centred on roads, private gardens and clearly defined front and back spaces".

Winding paths and planting weave between the blocks, connecting them and linking shared outdoor spaces.

She said she wanted it to be a public space people felt they could belong to.

"Housing needs to be progressive. People who live in the building have access to green space, allotments."

The site fronts on to Lion Green Road, with low-rise green belt housing set on higher ground to the south and traditional suburban streets to the north.

The project was funded by Croydon Council as a public asset, and a change in building regulations meant it "fought against five or six circumstantial elements beyond the normal challenges".

The building was praised by the jury for its "inventive and site-specific response to a highly constrained plot".

Buildings are assessed across a range of criteria, including design vision, innovation, sustainability, functionality, and the ability to delight users and visitors.

Entertainment.title: Off Campus star collaboration 'gave me chills', says Babydoll singer
Entertainment.text:
The singer behind the TikTok viral hit Babydoll says collaborating with an Off Campus star was "mind-boggling".

Jamie Miller, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, was close to calling it quits on his music career at the start of 2026, deciding it was his "last chance", financially and emotionally.

But over the summer everything changed when Babydoll caught the attention of people on social media, leading to a viral dance, his first UK top 10 single, and reaching number one in the US iTunes pop chart.

When Miller saw a comment from actor Antonio Cipriano, saying he "needed this song", he sent him a message suggesting he feature on a recording – then "panicked" and added "haha, joking".

"I'm a fan of Antonio's voice, and I have been a fan for a long time," he said.

"He messaged back and was like, 'If you're actually not joking, I'd be honoured'."

Cipriano headed to Los Angeles, where Miller now lives, and they recorded Babydoll on the day they first met, external.

"It was the best time ever," said Miller.

"We're coming up at the same time, he has an amazing career in acting and I feel like the stars aligned even for us to do this and the world is rallying around us as a duo too. The opportunities that we're having right now are incredible."

Amazon Prime Video's ice hockey romance series Off Campus – based on a book series by Elle Kennedy - has similarly taken the world by storm this year, ranking as the third most-watched series launch in the platform's history, external.

It has raised the profile of numerous artists, with a soundtrack merging old favourites with new music.

Asked if he would like to be involved with the series in future, Miller said: "I'm such a fan of the show. I think it's absolutely incredible what they're doing, what Antonio is doing. In any capacity, I would love to. We'll see."

On Friday, the original version of Babydoll moved from number three to number two in the official UK charts - beaten only by Taylor Swift's Patient Zero.

Miller also recently supported The Jonas Brothers on the US leg of their tour, and said bringing Cipriano out as a guest star at some of the shows was "mind-boggling".

"I think the easiest thing about it was we're doing it together, for the first time. It was his first arena, it was my first arena, and I think that's the most amazing situation to be in, because we can lean on each other.

"Backstage we would say to each other, 'we're so lucky, our lives are not normal, we're going out to play for 20,000 people, what are we doing bro?'.

"Introducing him gave me chills because, as well as my dreams coming true right now, his dreams are too.

"It's so nice and needed, to have a friend who can guide you through."

At 19, Miller competed in The Voice UK, coming third place with coach Jennifer Hudson.

But his love for music first began accidentally, when he took part in a primary school show.

"If you auditioned for the play, then you got to skip out math class," he recalled.

"Just to see the reaction from the teachers after they asked me to sing a song, was just absolutely like 'I want to do this, this is actually incredible.'

"All my mates were rugby players and football players, whereas I just wanted to do music. After that one audition, I was hooked."

Now 29, Miller admits the past couple of years have been "really tough", adding changes in the music industry and in his personal life had left him feeling quite lost.

"Going into this year was my last chance to try and cut through. This industry is really hard, it's really expensive as well," he said.

"I think the thing with success, people think you have a lot of money... I didn't really see that side of that. So financially, this year, I couldn't really make it work anymore. I was on my last legs."

Miller said he "never had any social media campaign" planned and it "happened the most organic way possible".

As the Babydoll dance took hold of social media, Miller collaborated with an array of stars including actors Jennifer Love Hewitt, Lucy Hale and Julianne Hough, as well as popstar Meghan Trainor.

"All these incredible people I've been able to do it with, they've said it themselves, they've said 'we needed this song'.

"From all sides of the world, it's kind of unified people in a way, and it's just a beautiful thing to be a part of something that made someone smile."

Miller said he was "proud" of his new music and was excited to share his latest album with the world and to tour it – in particular, he said, to bring it to Wales.

But he added the non-stop nature of the past couple of months had been "really hard to process".

"It feels like so many life changes are happening around me, but I'm still the same person. It's dystopian, in a way.

"Especially being from Wales, you don't really see stuff like this happening to people all the time. Tom Jones is absolutely incredible, but I feel like he's really been the one that's flown the flag, and rightfully so.

"I'm very appreciative for everything that's going on right now, and thank my lucky stars. I just hope I'm doing Wales proud, to be honest."

Entertainment.title: BBC News channel launches on YouTube for viewers in UK and US
Entertainment.text:
The BBC News channel has been made available to stream live on YouTube for viewers in the UK and USA.

The trial, which began on Thursday, external, has been described by BBC bosses as "a significant step" in expanding access to "trusted, impartial journalism in more places people use every day".

The move is an expansion of what the BBC has already done in other countries, with the news channel also available to YouTube viewers in Australia, Kenya, Nigeria, and Poland.

Broadening access to the service forms part of the BBC's wider strategy to reach digitally-native new and younger audiences.

The channel offers rolling coverage of international and domestic news, as well as breaking news and the latest developments in the worlds of politics, business, technology, culture and sport.

The BBC's YouTube strategy is widely seen a response to the increasing fragmentation of audiences.

The guarantees that viewers sit down and turn on their favourite channel - whatever is on it - are long gone.

Now, their TV sets take them into a world of infinite choice and the BBC (along with the UK's other public service broadcasters) knows it needs to go to where audiences are - as well as trying to entice them to its own platforms.

Thursday's development is part of the specific drive by the BBC to take its trusted news to audiences who aren't tuning in to the news channel directly or via the iPlayer.

BBC News's director of AI, innovation and growth, Anjali Kapoor, said in a statement that audiences "increasingly expect news to be available wherever they are, on the platforms they use throughout their day.

"Launching the BBC News channel on YouTube in the UK and US is an important step in bringing our trusted journalism to even more people."

She added: "It will make it easier for audiences to access live coverage of the stories shaping our world, while helping us reach new audiences in the places and at the times that work best for them."

The move is all part of the fight to combat the disinformation taking hold across social media and beyond.

But it also won't hurt in the continuing negotiations over the BBC's charter and its future funding after 2027.

This is another signal to the government that the BBC takes its mission seriously; that it is the place for trusted, impartial news and that it understands it must make that news available as widely as possible.

However, viewers in the UK, watching the channel live on YouTube, may not realise they still need a TV licence to do that.

But with no guardrails around who's watching, no ability - for now anyway - for the BBC to insist you prove you've paid the fee before you can access its YouTube channels (or its own streaming channels), it's going to be hard to enforce.

In July, the corporation's new director general described the traditional TV licence model as "a busted flush" and "no longer fit for purpose".

Former Google executive Matt Brittin told MPs that the licence fee is "yesterday's model".

He did not specify what he wants to replace it, but he and BBC chair Samir Shah suggested the government should reconsider a compulsory household levy, which it previously ruled out.

The BBC receives most of its funding from the £180-a-year TV licence, but the number of households paying has declined in recent years, and the broadcaster is discussing reform of the system with the government.

Entertainment.title: Inside Brooklyn novelty shop at centre of 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
Entertainment.text:
On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in a quiet part of New York City was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual.

Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby in this Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?"

Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall.

The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000).

"Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items.

In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable".

Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale.

It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000.

They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day.

"Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said.

"It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity."

Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception."

When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers.

A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual.

Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m.

The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!"

The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad killed suspect
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Some readers may find this article distressing.

An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class.

As she tussled with him on the floor of the class - where three children and a teacher were killed - a bystander armed with a pistol ran inside and killed the teen.

The bystander, a father of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend on Thursday lunchtime when he saw the suspect firing in the car park, then shooting through a window to enter.

Police said the 16-year-old suspect used to be a student at the school.

Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.

"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.

Police offered more information on the attack at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.

The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.

Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.

Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.

He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".

He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.

A search warrant has been executed at the suspect's home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.

Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but they are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.

Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.

But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.

The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.

Police said he had a legally concealed .40 calibre in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.

Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, California, told a local CBS station her son had called her moments after the shooting, and he was "traumatised".

"He said a man went into my daughter's school," Freeman said, pausing as she started to tear up. "And, um, shot kids. And he said, and I looked at him point blank, and I shot and killed him, mom."

She added: "I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, mom, I couldn't save them all."

US President Donald Trump praised the bystander on Friday, calling him a "great hero".

Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been "much worse" with no intervention.

"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.

Without naming the bystander, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".

Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Trump waives several Russian sanctions as new US law takes effect
BreakingNewsTab.text:
US President Donald Trump has used his presidential authority to block numerous sanctions on Russia that were recently passed by the US Congress in an effort to punish the country for its war on Ukraine.

In an executive order on Friday night, Trump said that it is in the US "national interests" to withhold some of the sanctions. Trump signed the sanctions bill into law in September, and it was due to take effect on Sunday.

It comes days after Trump said the US would import Russian diesel in an effort to bring down US energy prices before the midterm elections in November, which will decide which party controls Congress.

The plan shocked lawmakers, and has triggered a bipartisan backlash.

The US sanctions law is named for the late Republican South Carolina Senator Lindsey Graham, who was one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July.

The law took aim at Russian's economy, and gave Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.

Additionally, the law includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions.

On Thursday, a bipartisan group of 20 US lawmakers issued a letter calling on Trump to respect the new law, which is due to take effect on 18 October.

The lawmakers thanked Trump for signing the sanctions bill, and urged his "full and faithful implementation" of the law.

The lawmakers said it would be "decisive in forcing Putin to take peace talks seriously" and called on the Trump administration "to apply the Graham law's sanctions to their fullest extent and without delay".

Last week, Trump announced that he had held a phone call with Putin, and had agreed to purchase diesel from Moscow.

US allies criticised the move, anxious that it could help Russia in its war effort.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a gift to Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Zacharia was thrown into a whirlwind - and failed at a critical time for Trump
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The White House press secretary job is a challenging one, even under the best of circumstances.

These were not the best of circumstances.

Katie Zacharia was thrown into the whirlwind, joining the White House team as press secretary just weeks away from what polls suggest could be a difficult midterm congressional elections for President Donald Trump and his Republican Party.

In just five days, she was out – the result of a disastrous press conference that lasted all of 14 minutes, followed by a series of halting media appearances and questions about whether she had mischaracterised her legal credentials over the course of her career.

The axe dropped on Friday, with the news delivered – in a roundabout way - by Trump himself before the gathered media at the White House, as he recounted a conversation he had with Zacharia earlier in the day.

"Honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," Trump said he told Zacharia. "Katie, do you need this? I don't think you need this."

He later added that maybe the press secretary job "is not for her".

In case there was any doubt, the White House quickly confirmed to the BBC that Zacharia would be "transitioning" out of her current job.

Trump may be wondering whether Zacharia "needs" the press secretary job, but presidents – including this one - benefit most from a competent press secretary in times of crisis.

And while there may not be an immediate crisis, this White House is certainly facing growing adversity.

Across the US, Republican candidates are scrambling to hold on to their seats in the upcoming elections. Some are doing so by distancing themselves from the president and his policies, creating new stresses and faultlines within a party that has for so long been broadly unified behind Trump.

Meanwhile, the White House has been beset by a series of controversies – including allegations of corruption that forced the resignation of US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and an abrupt reversal of plans to publicly air a military execution in December after widespread bipartisan backlash.

A skilled press secretary may have been able to navigate these political landmines while continuing to push out the White House's preferred message in the face of a building media frenzy.

Karoline Leavitt, who worked as Trump's press secretary from the start of his second term until she resigned in August a few months after welcoming her second child, proved highly adept at defending the administration from the press room lectern while avoiding stumbles and maintaining a collegial relationship with journalists.

Her performance set a high bar for Zacharia, who was a relative novice. It was a mark she failed to reach or even approach, although she never really had much of a chance.

The speed at which she failed was astounding, setting a modern record for the shortest-tenured White House press secretary.

Zacharia's halting Tuesday press conference performance, combined with those questions about her legal background, essentially sealed her fate.

And subsequent press appearances, including a less-than-welcoming interview with conservative pundit Sean Hannity on Thursday – which Trump said he watched – did nothing to change that.

As president, Trump has essentially acted as his own press secretary, making major announcements and changing policies from the Oval Office, the White House lawn, airfield tarmacs – wherever he happens to be.

Zacharia herself noted this phenomenon prior to being tabbed for the White House job. "President Trump does not need a spokesperson," she posted on X. "He is his own best press secretary."

Now, he will have to be.

Trump's penchant for speaking off the cuff, however, has made the job a difficult one over the course of his two terms in office.

His press secretaries have sometimes had their public statements undermined by presidential pronouncements. At other times, they've been left out of the loop of key decisions.

When they have been effective, they have managed to ride the choppier waves while also smoothing relations with the media - providing context for inquisitive journalists and helping tamp down any simmering issues.

In comments to Fox News on Friday, Trump said that he is in "no rush" to find a new press secretary. But at such a critical time in his second term, Trump will be without the help that someone like Leavitt offered so consistently.

He may come to regret not having it.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Chris Mason: Burnham and Swinney tussle over where power lies in Scotland
BreakingNewsTab.text:
UK political debate has had a distinctly Scottish feel these last few days.

As the Scottish National Party has gathered for its annual conference at the Event Complex on the outskirts of Aberdeen, the Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has been in Paisley and Edinburgh and the prime minister has been in Motherwell.

The SNP is buoyant, its activists gathering for the first time since it won, in May, a fifth consecutive Scottish Parliament election, albeit with fewer seats than they won in 2021.

Next year will mark the moment the party has been in devolved power at Holyrood for 20 years.

It is quite the contrast with where the SNP found itself just two years ago, pulverised by the landslide at the general election in 2024 where Labour gained 36 seats from the SNP.

As I wrote a year ago, the SNP's critics point to what they see as a dismal domestic record, on the NHS and the number of deaths among drug addicts, for instance.

The SNP counter Scotland has more police officers per person than England and Wales and the highest spend per school pupil in the UK.

No matter the arguments, the result in May was clear - the SNP leader and First Minister John Swinney has his own mandate. Little wonder, given the state of the party when he took the job, that the conference brochure has a front page photo of a smiling Swinney cradling a glass of whisky.

And remember it wasn't just an electoral pummelling the SNP was dealing with, but the jaw dropping details which culminated in the jailing of Peter Murrell, the party's former chief executive - and estranged husband of the former First Minister Nicola Sturgeon - for embezzling more than £400,000 from the party.

Swinney now looks ahead to a parliamentary term with all that behind them and a new prime minister to deal with in Downing Street.

Burnham and Swinney share a diagnosis that Westminster has failed to deliver and political power is better administered closer to people than it ever has been.

But, crucially, the prime minister sees the "drama" of the constant questions around Scottish independence as a distraction.

For Swinney, independence has been and remains his lifelong political goal.

We have had a glimpse this week as to how that dynamic between the two men may play out.

Burnham's critics, including the SNP, have seen this former Mancunian mayor's devolutionary instincts as having a distinctly English flavour. The prime minister, on his trip to New College Lanarkshire, sought to counter that.

"I do want a good growth in every postcode here, and in the rest of the UK, and I want to work with the first minister to deliver it. We won't agree on everything, but we can agree on something," he said.

"I want us to design a new model together of regional economic empowerment across Scotland, one that puts control in the hands of local people."

Burnham has offered to devolve powers on localised employment support, currently held by the Department of Work and Pensions.

Both he and the Secretary of State for Scotland, Douglas Alexander, said Scotland was "one of the most centralised nations in Europe", an assertion flatly rejected by Swinney.

Scotland's first minister has said he wants "much more opportunity for a regional dimension to take forward skills, economic opportunity and planning" and his team acknowledge this vision includes overlaps with the regional combined authorities seen in parts of England, albeit without mayors.

It will be intriguing to observe, given the rivalry and grit that exists between Labour and the SNP, how things develop beyond the prime minister's speech.

Here in Aberdeen, activists have seized upon the prime minister's reflections on Brexit to argue that if he can revisit the outcome of the referendum in 2016 on the European Union, Scots should be able to revisit the one in 2014 on independence.

There have been plenty of mentions too of an exchange in the Commons last month between SNP MP Chris Law and Andy Burnham, when Burnham suggested another Scottish independence referendum could be held, if public opinion showed demand for one.

SNP folk think - perhaps hope - this represents the prime minister's authentic view.

He and Downing Street have seen sought to squash this idea and he said he wanted to "move on" from a debate about Scottish independence.

Privately, senior SNP figures accept the authority to sanction another referendum lies with Westminster and the UK government says no. So, their focus is seeking to steadily build the case for independence in how they choose to govern.

Within the party, a new group called, you guessed it, "Independence" has been set up.

Speaking at its launch event, the SNP's former Policy Convener Toni Giugliano argued that "countries don't become independent by waiting for permission. They do so when support becomes unstoppable and when a national consensus for change is built".

Furthermore, he argued, fundamental questions about what an independent Scotland would look and feel like must be answered now - such as the currency that would be used and how the state pension would work.

These are the long term questions.

For now, the tussle is more short term, as the SNP ponders when the prime minister might call a general election.

Buoyed by its recent victory at Holyrood, the party senses Labour vulnerability in the swathe of seats Labour took from them two years ago.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Trump 'completely wrong' to restrict support for Ukraine, Italian minister tells BBC
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Italy's defence minister has said it is a "complete mistake, a major mistake" for the US to limit access to satellite systems and intelligence used by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

In a BBC interview, Guido Crosetto warned that any such move by US President Donald Trump's administration "makes absolutely no sense" and risked prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping to bring peace.

US officials have said Trump has not asked for the slowdown of internet speeds the US provides to Ukraine and which are vital for its war effort. Trump has also denied that the US has stopped sharing early-warning alerts of incoming Russian aerial attacks with Ukraine.

Crosetto's comments continue Italy's sharpening criticism of the US.

Earlier this week, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called Trump's deal to buy diesel from Russia a "very risky choice", and said it would "grant Russia legitimacy" as it bombed cities in Ukraine.

Trump agreed the deal with Vladimir Putin, blaming Kyiv's own attacks on Russian refineries for rising fuel prices.

Meloni, once considered so close to the US president she was dubbed a "Trump whisperer", said the move ran counter to efforts to bring Putin to the negotiating table.

"Peace will come when Putin is convinced there is a stalemate, that he cannot advance any further," her defence minister told the BBC at his ministry building in Rome.

Crosetto was a co-founder of Meloni's hard-right Fratelli d'Italia party, which has led a right-wing government coalition since 2022, shortly after the start of Russia's full-scale war.

"If [Putin] sees weakness on the Ukrainian side – and if the US deprives Ukraine of resources, that creates weakness – then he will believe he can win. So he will continue the war," Crosetto warned.

"I think that is completely wrong."

That party's leader, former general Roberto Vannacci, is openly sympathetic to Russia and opposes aiding Ukraine, arguing that Europe is wasting its money as Russia's military "continues to advance" on the ground.

At a recent event in Tuscany, he described himself as "neither pro-Putin nor pro-Russian" but "pro-Italian".

Crosetto brushed off questions about Vannacci, including on whether his views reflected those of many Italians, saying he had more "serious matters to deal with".

But, perhaps to underline the difference, he was unequivocal on Russia.

"When one state crosses another state's border with tanks, when it bombs hospitals and schools, kills civilians and bombs power plants, and has been doing so for four years, I can only describe that as evil," he said.

But Italians, like many Europeans, are seeing prices go up, driven by the high cost of energy.

During street protests in Rome on Friday, where firecrackers were thrown, secondary school students complained that resources were being diverted to arms, instead of education.

Some chanted: "We want more classroom, not more bombs."

In southern Italy, truckers have begun blocking roads complaining at the hike in fuel prices.

Polls here regularly show that a majority of Italians want an end to military aid for Ukraine. One, conducted for the Ixè institute in September, put support for continuing to supply arms at just 18%.

There are many factors behind that, from a long-standing pacifist tradition to a history of strong business ties to Moscow. Unlike Poland or the Baltic states, Italy feels physically distant from the danger, too.

But the defence minister also blamed an active campaign of disinformation by Moscow – targeting, he said, "certain political figures... and narratives to weaken the political climate against Russia".

"In some way they shift public opinion," the minister argued.

"It's very hard to explain to a citizen who's having trouble at the petrol pump that we can't give any concessions to Russia right now. But that's the only way to defend the future of that very citizen who's complaining."

Italy has not been targeted for major acts of sabotage, unlike other allies of Ukraine in Europe.

The minister said a fire at an arms depot outside Rome in August was not arson, but "human stupidity".

A report last month that Russia was planning to launch drone attacks at Italy, France and Spain from the container ships in the Mediterranean was not proven, Crosetto also told us.

But cyber-attacks, which he linked to Russia, were now routine - "there are hundreds every day" - and he believed Europe had been too weak in its response.

"You can't win a war... if you don't fight back," the minister said.

With additional reporting from Rome by Davide Ghiglione.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Tiger attack victim's medical records may have been breached
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Medical records belonging to a man killed by a tiger at Yorkshire Wildlife Park may have been accessed "without a legitimate reason" by staff at Yorkshire Ambulance Service, a spokesperson has said.

William Chapman, 24, was mauled to death at the park near Doncaster on Saturday.

In a statement, the trust said following Chapman's death it had identified two possible incidents of staff "accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information" about the case.

It said an investigation had been launched "to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches".

Chapman died as a result of "multiple traumatic injuries and animal interaction" after entering the tiger's enclosure at the park, an inquest into his death heard on Thursday.

In a statement, a spokesperson for Yorkshire Ambulance Service NHS Trust said Chapman's family was aware of the potential breach and offered their condolences to his relatives.

They said: "We believe there may have been two instances involving two members of staff accessing or attempting to access incident/medical information following this incident without a legitimate reason to do so.

"We take the confidentiality and security of patient information extremely seriously and have robust systems in place to protect information, and this concern has been identified as a result of our proactive audits.

"The trust has commenced an investigation to establish the full circumstances surrounding these potential breaches and the actions of these individuals.

"We have also reported this matter to the Information Commissioner's Office and we will continue to keep William's family informed as our investigation progresses."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Police feared Andrew might delay access by saying his home was King's
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Thames Valley Police feared Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor might have tried to stop officers entering his home in Sandringham by saying it belonged to the King, according to legal documents.

Senior officers were concerned the King's brother could argue it was not his property, and that separate legal permission would have to be sought before officers could enter it.

Delaying access would have risked the loss of evidence, the force said.

The background to Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest in February has emerged in legal documents, when police asked a judge for warrants to raid the former prince's homes.

Lawyers for Mountbatten-Windsor successfully argued those warrants were unlawful in court last week.

Mountbatten-Windsor's arrest came after the US Department of Justice published material which showed his connections to the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The BBC has approached Mountbatten-Windsor's representatives for comment and he has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein.

The arrest of the former prince, on 19 February, was on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

On 18 February, Thames Valley Police asked for permission from the Central Criminal Court for warrants to search Wood Farm in Sandringham and Royal Lodge in Windsor.

The request included the police outlining the scenarios in which they believed they would need search warrants to ensure access to the properties.

They feared that Mountbatten-Windsor or his legal team would want to see "judicial authority" before allowing the police to enter, the documents show.

The police were concerned that Mountbatten-Windsor or his representatives could argue that the Sandringham Estate was the property of King Charles - and that it would be a slow process getting a separate right of access.

Such a delay would "frustrate the nature and purpose of the search," said the police, in their application for search warrants.

There was also a concern that no one would be present at the property and that media attention could be drawn to the police presence outside while not being able to enter.

Any of those delays could have meant the police would have been unable to gather the evidence they wanted, they argued - and "given the gravity of this investigation", the police asked for search warrants.

In separate documents filed as part of Mountbatten-Windsor's legal challenge against the warrants, his lawyers said: "These assertions were no more than speculation."

The documents also detail the type of information the police were seeking inside the properties.

They say: "Paper-work, diaries, business records or other documentary evidence of AMW's [Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's] time as Special Representative for Trade and Investment.

"Further evidence as to any action, communication, comment or in relation to matters following the release of material by the FBI concerning the late Jeffrey Epstein as AMW will be aware that Thames Valley Police is conducting an assessment.

"Specifically mobile phone(s) and computer(s) [to include electronic notebooks, surfaces, iPads and any older electronic devices," which could have held information about links to Epstein at the time when Mountbatten-Windsor had been the UK's trade envoy."

The documents show the search of Royal Lodge, Mountbatten-Windsor's former home in Windsor, continued until 24 February.

They also reveal his police interview at Aylesham Police Station began at 15:00 GMT and he was released under investigation at 18:36.

The legal documents give details of why the police wanted to talk to Mountbatten-Windsor, including the claim that when he was a UK trade envoy he had forwarded Jeffrey Epstein official reports from official visits to Singapore, Vietnam, China and Hong Kong.

There was also a claim, arising from emails in the Epstein files released in the US, that Mountbatten-Windsor had briefed Epstein on investment opportunities in Afghanistan.

Also mentioned is the suggestion Mountbatten-Windsor held meetings with a private investment firm and then suggesting to Epstein that he might invest in the company.

The legal documents have emerged after a High Court hearing earlier this month in which Thames Valley Police accepted the warrants it used to search Mountbatten-Windsor's homes were unlawful.

Mountbatten-Windsor's lawyers used a judicial review to successfully challenge the actions of the force's chief constable and the Central Criminal Court in the build-up to his arrest.

Thames Valley Police's position was that they had applied for search warrants under section eight and nine of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 at a hearing at the Central Criminal Court the day before the search.

That court determined that only section eight search warrants were needed and they were granted on that basis - but subsequently, a legal challenge has established that the court should have issued them under the section nine.

But items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.

Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.

Thames Valley Police force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.

At the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.

However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.

Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.

Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.

As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.

BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.

Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.

Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.

The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".

The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.

The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.

Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.

Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".

The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.

Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.

These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Three men jailed for 158 years each for murdering Australian brothers and US friend in Mexico
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A Mexican judge has sentenced three men convicted of murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, and their US friend Carter Rhoad to 158 years and nine months in jail each.

The Robinsons and Rhoad were killed in an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California in 2024 while they were on a surfing trip, the court heard during the trial.

The murders sent shockwaves around the world, particularly in Australia, as the area is usually safe from the violence seen in other parts of Mexico.

The guilty verdict was handed down last week. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the courtroom that her sons' murders had taken "the future we had imagined with them".

The convicted killers' full names could not be given for legal reasons, and they were only identified as Jesús Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Ángel Jesús.

In November last year, the girlfriend of the alleged ringleader, Jesús Gerardo (alias "El Kekas"), was sentenced in a separate trial to 20 years in prison. She had admitted to involvement in the robbery.

The court heard that the bodies of the victims were found dumped down a well with gunshot wounds to their heads.

At the time, the murders shocked locals and tourists in the beach town of Ensenada who were disturbed at the apparent ease and sheer pointlessness of the killings.

Ensenada has a reputation as a welcoming spot for surfers, but the chilling murders revealed how commonplace such extreme violence remains in Mexico.

The only explanation the authorities were able to give was that the surfers - all in their early 30s - had ultimately been murdered for being in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Their killings happened barely 36 hours after they crossed into Mexico from the US. Their bodies, however, were not found for another week, when their families were able to identify them.

Local surfers also called for greater security for residents and visiting tourists, citing other recent examples of violence in the state. Tourism is a key part of the regional economy in Baja California.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Palestinians and US journalist injured by Israeli settlers in West Bank harvest attack
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Dozens of masked settlers have attacked Palestinians and set fire to cars and olive trees during the annual olive harvest in the occupied West Bank.

A BBC team witnessed one of several attacks in farmland near the Palestinian village of Abu Falah. A local official said the attacks had injured 12 Palestinians, including four dual Palestinian American citizens. A foreign journalist was also among those hurt.

Driving into the area early in the morning, we came across the first signs of the violence: a stream of cars carrying wounded Palestinian olive farmers racing out along the narrow stony track, piled high with olive picking equipment, as smoke rose from several fires nearby.

The bloodied face of Majdi Fheed peered out from the backseat of one car.

"We were getting our olive trees and almost 15 Jewish guys … started attacking us with guns, with rocks, with special weapons. They hit me on my head [and] my neck – look, I am bleeding!"

Yaser AlKam, a council member from the neighbouring village of Turmus Aya told me Majdi - an American citizen - was attacked by settlers with nail-studded sticks, and needed treatment for deep wounds on his head. His elderly mother was also injured.

Another man ferrying the injured to hospital told us that settlers had attacked them with sticks while they harvested their olives, and had burned three cars – including one of his own.

"As soon as we got to the land and put our things on the ground, they started to come, so we ran away" said a woman next to him.

Asked about the violence, a US State Department spokesperson said they were aware of the reports.

"We condemn criminal violence by any party in the West Bank and call for investigations, arrests, and convictions, of those responsible," the spokesperson said.

Watching the vehicles stream past her, 73-year-old Imm Khaldoun told me emphatically that, no matter what happened, she would always return to her land. "This is my land. It's my right [to be here]" she told me.

The UN says the past two weeks have already seen more attacks by violent Israeli settlers than during the entire harvest season last year.

Olive picking in the West Bank is now a test of speed, with trees rapidly stripped of fruit as soon as the sun rises, before violent Israeli settlers attack.

In another olive orchard nearby, we watched as dozens of farmers used power-tools to strip the trees as fast as they could – one eye on the ridge above us, where a group of settlers at a new illegal outpost had already gathered, and were watching the olive harvest below.

Standing on ladders, the Palestinian farmers worked quickly, sending streams of olives onto the plastic sheets laid out under the trees. Three villages had come together to harvest these olives, the landowner Amin Khalil, told me, as a form of protection against attack. He said his land was now surrounded by seven Jewish settlements and outposts.

All Israeli settlements are illegal under international law. Outposts – small encampments on hilltops – are illegal under Israeli law as well, but many still receive state support.

"This is a hotspot – there are seven settlements around here," Amin Khalil told me. "This year, all the people came together because when there are just a few people working alone at the edge of the village, the settlers attack. So all the families are working together today."

But the tactic doesn't work today. As we watch, dozens of settlers, all dressed in black, begin moving down the hill towards us, setting fire to several groups of olive trees.

There are shouts of panic from the Palestinian farmers, yelling for children to get out of the field. Some begin swiftly wrapping up the olives to leave.

But with large numbers of people on both sides, the confrontation stalls into an uneasy stalemate. We see settlers with slingshots hurl stones towards us, and young Palestinian men running to throw stones in return.

As Israeli forces arrive, the standoff explodes into action. Settlers begin running down towards us as the farmers swiftly retreat. Some Palestinians set off fireworks to try and push the settlers back.

American journalist Heidi Levine of the Washington Post was injured in the attack. She described how dozens of settlers ambushed her as she was reporting at the scene.

"I got jumped," she said. "I was on the ground and they were kicking me and I was trying to hold onto my camera and my bag. I had my helmet and flak jacket on which protected me. They made me stand up and they kicked me again, and this went on for at least 10 minutes."

In a statement, Washington Post executive editor Matt Murray said Levine had been clearly identifiable as a journalist.

"We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thorough investigation and follow-through from authorities," he said.

Despite the video evidence and testimony, the Israeli prime minister's office said the facts remained unclear and were under investigation.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said personnel had been despatched to the area "following a report of a violent confrontation". It said a female journalist had been injured during the confrontation. And that "all circumstances" surrounding the incident would be examined.

As the farmers retreated, the sound of live ammunition cracked across the fields. It was unclear if settlers or Israeli forces were firing.

Minutes later, Israeli forces began firing tear gas into the Palestinian fields to end the confrontation – a well-worn Israeli pattern of managing these conflicts.

The UN says settler attacks on the olive harvest this year have so far killed one Palestinian and injured more than 120 others across the West Bank.

Illegal Jewish outposts have mushroomed here over the past few years, clustering in closer around Palestinian olive groves.

What we witnessed was part of a pattern being repeated day after day, as settler outposts here increase.

The yearly olive harvest has become a litmus test of how the policies of Israel's fiercely pro-settlement government are affecting Palestinians here, by presiding over growing violence by extremist settlers, and fuelling Jewish claims to the land.
